prompt: Put the four counts in the order `confusion_matrix(...).ravel()` returns them for a yes-or-no problem.
hint: Rows are the truth, columns the prediction, negatives first.

prompt: Lowering the cut from 0.5 to 0.278 moves rows between cells. Which moves happen?

choices.text: Leavers become stayers
choices.why: The truth does not change with the cut.

choices.text: Nothing moves; the counts depend on the model only
choices.why: The counts only exist once a cut is chosen.

choices.text: True positives become false negatives, because fewer people are now called leavers
choices.why: That is raising the cut.

choices.text: Missed leavers become caught ones; some stayers become wasted credits
choices.why: Yes. 117 to 348 true positives, 77 to 363 false positives.

prompt: At the cut of 0.278: 348 true positives, 363 false positives. How many credits are sent?
Why does accuracy barely move across cuts on this data?

choices.text: The true negatives dominate it
choices.why: Yes. 94% of rows are stayers, and accuracy counts every row the same.

choices.text: Accuracy ignores false positives
choices.why: It counts them as wrong, like every other error.

choices.text: scikit-learn rounds it to three decimals
choices.why: The rounding is in the print; the values really are close.

choices.text: The model is too weak to change anything at any cut
choices.why: Its net value moves from R$ 1,848 to R$ 23,448 across the same cuts.

prompt: In which of these is accuracy a sensible metric?

choices.text: Fraud, at one transaction in a thousand
choices.why: A model saying *never fraud* scores 99.9%.

choices.text: Apples against oranges, half of each, both errors harmless
choices.why: Yes. Balanced classes and equal costs are its conditions.

choices.text: Churn at 6% a month, where a missed leaver and a wasted credit cost different amounts
choices.why: This lesson's whole point is that it fails there.

choices.text: A rare disease screened across a large population, mostly healthy
choices.why: Rare class, unequal costs.

prompt: Match each metric to its question.
hint: Precision looks at what was sent; recall at who was leaving.

pairs.right: Of the credits sent, how many reached a leaver?
Of the leavers, how many got a credit?
Of the stayers, how many got a credit?

right_distractors: Of all rows, how many were right?

prompt: At a cut of 0.5: 117 true positives, 77 false positives. What is the precision? Three decimal places.
At a cut of 0.5: 117 true positives, 1,367 false negatives. What is the recall? Three decimal places.
A vendor reports a churn model with a recall of 0.92 and nothing else. What do you ask first?

choices.text: Nothing; 0.92 is excellent
choices.why: Without a cut and a precision it is unreadable.

choices.text: Which algorithm it uses
choices.why: The algorithm does not tell you whether 0.92 is worth anything.

choices.text: At what cut, and with what precision?
choices.why: Yes. A low enough cut gives any recall, by sending nearly everybody a credit.

choices.text: Whether the recall is above 0.9 on the training months too
choices.why: Training scores say even less.

prompt: Precision 0.5, recall 0.2. What is the F1 score? Three decimal places.
At the cut of 0.1, F1 is 0.359, almost the best, while net value collapses to R$ 1,848. Why does F1 not see it?
hint: What does F1 assume about the two errors?

choices.text: F1 cannot be computed below a cut of 0.2, so the table shows a stale value
choices.why: It is computed at 0.1 in the same table.

choices.text: F1 only measures precision
choices.why: It combines precision and recall.

choices.text: It is computed on the training months
choices.why: Same test rows as the net value.

choices.text: It weighs both errors alike and ignores true negatives
choices.why: Yes. Here a wasted credit and a missed leaver cost different amounts.

prompt: Why is F1 a harmonic mean rather than the ordinary average of precision and recall?

choices.text: It punishes a model hopeless at either one
choices.why: Yes. The ordinary average would give that model about 0.5; the harmonic, 0.02.

choices.text: It always equals accuracy
choices.why: It ignores true negatives, which accuracy counts.

choices.text: It is faster to compute than a plain average
choices.why: Both take no time.

choices.text: It weighs recall twice as much as precision
choices.why: That would be F2.

prompt: What are the two axes of a ROC curve?
hint: Two rates, one for each class.

choices.text: Precision across, recall up
choices.why: That is the other curve, in section 08.

choices.text: False positive rate across, true positive rate up
choices.why: Yes. Every cut is a point.

choices.text: Time across, the score up
choices.why: No time in it.

choices.text: The cut across, and the net value at that cut up the side
choices.why: That would be useful, but it is not the ROC curve.

prompt: What does the diagonal of the ROC chart represent?
hint: Same share of each class at every cut.

choices.text: A perfect model, one that ranks every leaver first
choices.why: Perfect is the top left corner.

choices.text: The curve of the training months
choices.why: Only test rows are drawn.

choices.text: A model that knows nothing
choices.why: Yes. It reaches leavers and stayers at the same rate.

choices.text: The break-even cut, where a credit pays for itself
choices.why: A cut is a point, not a line.

prompt: An AUC of 0.804 means what, in words?

choices.text: 80.4% of leavers get a credit
choices.why: That is a recall, which needs a cut.

choices.text: The model is 80.4% calibrated
choices.why: AUC ignores calibration altogether.

choices.text: 80.4% of predictions are correct
choices.why: That would be accuracy at some cut.

choices.text: A random leaver outscores a random stayer 80.4% of the time
choices.why: Yes. AUC is about ranking only.

prompt: AUC depends only on the ___ of the scores, so multiplying every score by two leaves it unchanged.
On the precision-recall chart, the model that knows nothing sits at the share of positives. What is it on the test months, to three decimals?
Why prefer average precision to ROC AUC when comparing churn models?

choices.text: It is driven by the top of the ranking, where credits are sent
choices.why: Yes. AUC weighs the order among the bottom twenty thousand just as much.

choices.text: It is always higher
choices.why: Here it is far lower, 0.322 against 0.804.

choices.text: It needs a cut, and cuts are more realistic
choices.why: It needs no cut.

choices.text: ROC AUC fails to compute on rare classes
choices.why: It can; it just flatters the model there.

hint: The business question has its own metric.

Does it rank leavers above stayers?

prompt: Which of these reports follows the lesson's habits?
hint: Business metric first, the cut stated.

choices.text: "Recall 0.33."
choices.why: No cut, no precision, no money.

choices.text: "R$ 23,448 at a cut of 0.2, with precision 0.42 and recall 0.33."
choices.why: Yes. The money, how it was made, and where.

choices.text: "Accuracy 0.941, the best of the five cuts."
choices.why: The most accurate cut makes less money.

choices.text: "AUC 0.804, so the model is ready."
choices.why: Ranking says nothing about the money at any cut.

prompt: The break-even cut, 0.278, made R$ 21,672, and a cut of 0.2 made R$ 23,448. What does that suggest?
hint: If chances were honest probabilities, which cut would win?

choices.text: The costs in `feira.py` are wrong
choices.why: The costs are given; the model's probabilities are what is in question.

choices.text: A cut of 0.2 is always best for churn
choices.why: The best cut depends on costs and calibration, not on churn in general.

choices.text: The model's chances are not quite honest probabilities
choices.why: Yes. With calibrated chances the break-even cut would win by construction; lesson 11.

choices.text: Nothing; the difference is a rounding error
choices.why: R$ 1,776 is not rounding.

prompt: Which of these metrics need a cut? Choose all that apply.
hint: The ones made from the four counts.

choices.text: ROC AUC
choices.why: It summarises every cut at once.

choices.text: Average precision
choices.why: It also summarises every cut.

choices.text: F1
choices.why: Yes, it combines two cut-dependent metrics.

choices.text: Precision
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Net value
choices.why: Yes. Credits are sent at a cut.
